title: Dharmin Parikh & Himaanshu Gupta: Behind One Useful Answer—Uber’s Earner Assistant

segments.text: Hey everyone. I'm Darmin and this is
Himanshu.
It's exciting to be here. We're going to
talk about how we built Uber assistant
for drivers and couriers.
So, a couple of weeks ago, our CEO Dara
posted this conversation between a
driver, a real driver, and our
assistant.
The driver was waiting for 33 minutes
without getting a trip.
And I asked our assistant the question,
"Give me better trips, my man."
And the assistant came up with a really
good recommendation.
If the answer of the interaction is very
simple, but there's a lot to unpack in
this answer.
So, today we're going to talk about how
our assistant really helps our drivers
and couriers.

talk into three parts. First, I'm going
to talk about what our drivers and

Then Himanshu will talk about the
implementation.

close it up with how we're making our

let's go back to the driver interaction

who has been waiting 33 minutes for a
trip,
you know, they see in the demand heat

time
and converts them into insights for the

This is one question that we're

It needs to measure the outcome. If
there was a recommendation, the
assistant needs to measure whether the
driver took that recommendation,
or whether it led to a success for them,

the next future recommendation should
look like.
So, this is the type of North Star that
we are shooting towards when we're
building the driver assistant. And now,
Himanshu will talk about the
implementation of how we are making it
real.

agent is only as good as its context.

query such as, "Where can I find trips?"
the agent needs to understand the
marketplace conditions, it needs to
understand the driver, and it needs to
understand the app activity. So, in this
case, there a bunch of data that existed

was not in a form that's readily
consumable by AI agents.
So, some of the foundational work that
we did was around building the APIs and
the aggregation pipelines that can turn
the marketplace data into actionable
insights.
So, having the data is one thing, but
it's really important how we expose that
data to the agent.
And that's where intelligent tool design
comes in.
Instead of exposing the raw APIs to the
agent, we actually designed tools around
the tasks that the agent is trying to
accomplish.
So, a very naive way to do this would be
what's on the left. They're a bunch of
APIs that the model can access. So, in
this case, it would make six calls to
these APIs.
It will need to understand the schema,
reconcile the location and time context,

while that's certainly doable, it's not
the best use of models inference and
reasoning capabilities to do something
that's deterministic in code.
And that's where an agent-ready tool
comes in.
So, as an example, we built a tool get
nearby opportunities. So, here the agent
just puts in the context into the tool
around the driver location, time,
preferences, and the search radius.
And the tool outputs a ranked list of
opportunities near the driver, and then
the model can do what it's really good
at. It can understand the user's intent.
It can understand like what are the
various options and weigh them, and then
show a good recommendation to the
driver.
So, that's our philosophy. Reduce the
Reduce what the model has to infer
before it can reason.
And now that we have these
good tools at its disposal, the next
step is how do we balance the trade-offs
between cost, latency, and quality?
So, our agent app architecture actually
supports multiple execution paths based
on the task at hand.
There's a fast path, and
on the left there's a good example, and
this is really suited for very
high-frequency
experiences such as embedded AI insights
on the driver home screen
on the session summary.
And for these scenarios, the context is
very clear. We exactly know what the
answer should be, so we can aggressively
optimize for latency and cost.
The other end of the spectrum is where
the driver has a complex query.
Uh the driver asks the agent, "Help me
come up with a plan for the next week so
that I can earn $1,500."
That's a complex task that requires deep
reasoning. The model needs to understand
the driver's goals, the constraints,
marketplace forecast over the next week,
weather options, and then come up with a
good plan to show to the driver.
So, these sort of queries are not very
frequent, so we actually have the luxury
of taking more time and compute to
really get the quality high.
One thing that I really want to
highlight is that the most important
thing on this slide is the bar at the
bottom. So, even though these are
separate execution paths, but it's still
a single system. All of these execution
paths share the same foundation in terms
of the skills and the tools, context
engine, router guardrails, eval, etc.
One thing to keep in mind is that as the
agent has more flexibility, it's really
important to ensure that it operates
within the right boundaries.
And that's where guardrails come in and
are super critical.
So, we apply guardrails in both
directions, input uh for the user and
output the response that we show back.
On the input side, we monitor for
jailbreak, prompt injection, and other
adversarial scenarios. And on the
output, we ensure that the response
meets our safety criteria and our comms
policy.
And at Uber, instead of each and every
team building out these guardrails in a
bespoke manner, we have built a
centralized service called AI Guard.
This is a very simplistic high-level
architecture of AI Guard.
Uh AI Guard runs on all inputs that come
in from the user before they are sent
into the model, and it runs on all
outputs before they are shown to the
user.
And AI Guard is model agnostic. It can
work with proprietary third-party
models, open source models, or in-house
models.
And also for narrow classification
tasks, we use very small fine-tuned open
source models, which actually shows
strong performance with very low latency
and very low cost.
So now with AI Guard, we have the
confidence to deploy these agents in the
real world safely. The next question is
that how do we make sure that these
agents get better over time?
And that's why we have a couple of key
flywheels working for us. The first is a
quality loop. So here, as we get more
conversations, we understand some of the
failure modes, we fix the issues, and we
redeploy the improved agent.
The second one is the opportunity loop.
Here, the drivers are constantly telling
us what they want from the assistant,
and we can understand what are their
unmet needs, and then we can craft our
road map to meet those demands going
forward.
So let's double click on the quality
loop
for the next couple of slides with
real-world examples.
So with AI, the failures can be um
can manifest in very subtle ways.
The answer can look pretty reasonable,
but be factually wrong. Here is an
example of a real-world conversation.
The driver has some question about the
airport. We give a pretty good answer,
and then they have a follow-up about the
next hour.
So in this case, the agent actually
preserved the location context, but
dropped the time context.
But on the face of it, the output
response looks pretty reasonable.
But we have a bunch of LLM judges that
are trying to evaluate the conversation
quality across multiple dimensions such
as accuracy, conciseness, fidelity, etc.
And in this case, the LLM judge for
accuracy flagged an error because the
data was available on the back end, but
the model made an error with the tool
calling, and we fixed the issue and
deployed it.
But interestingly, all failure modes are
not related to accuracy.
The answer could be correct, but still
wrong in the moment.
Here's another example that I may have
talked about before.
The driver is a little bit frustrated.
It says
he says, "Give me better tips, my man."
And the agent earlier would give a good

if we really want to build an assistant
that feels like a companion to the
drivers, it's not just important to
answer the the wrong question, but but

So in this case, even a short

Now that we have these LLM judges, how
do we make sure that
we can run these evals in production at

So at a very high level, we have two
loops running.

But very importantly, we need to make

that's a loop at the bottom.
In order to have strong AI to human
alignment, we need to make sure that
there's good clean human input.

think in many scenarios.
Especially for scenarios around empathy,
conciseness, tone, there's there's a lot
of subjectivity.
And different humans might have
different opinions. So here's one
example where the driver asked where to
get trips now.
The agent gave a good factual answer and

It inferred the intent based on the

frustration, so should the agent
actually volunteer this empathetic
response?
So my broad point here is that it's

So so far I've talked about the various
building blocks of the system starting

box and
give the drivers help where they are in

Thaman is going to talk about next.
>> Cool. So
you know, as Himanshu talked about the
assistant, the assistant is only as
useful as the user invokes if it is just
reactive. We are making the assistant
proactive by bringing it in the app
where the users need the most. So there
are three moments that I would talk
about. First moment is when the user is
about to go online or is thinking about
going online. That's when the assistant
comes in and proactively surfaces
insights
to to talk about, "Hey, is this a good

this intervention. Second is when the

and it can only be used when the driver
